topic: Cost and latency engineering: prompt caching, batching, smaller models
why: The moment an AI deployment leaves pilot, the customer's finance team gets an invoice and their users get a spinner, and both land on the FDE. Nobody renews a system that costs $4 per ticket and takes eleven seconds to first token, and 'use a cheaper model' is not an answer you can give without evidence that quality held. This topic is the difference between an FDE who says 'we could try Haiku' and one who walks into the QBR with a table showing 62% lower cost per resolved ticket, p95 first-token down from 4.1s to 900ms, and an eval delta of -0.6 points inside the noise band.
prerequisites: LLM fundamentals (topic 45): tokenisation, context windows, and the fact that output tokens are priced roughly 5x input tokens - the whole cost model collapses if you reason in 'characters' or 'requests'.

Evals as infrastructure (topic 53): a versioned eval set with per-category breakdowns and a CI gate, because every cost reduction in this topic is only shippable if you can prove the quality delta is inside the noise band.

LLM observability (topic 54): per-request spans carrying model id, token counts and latency, so you have the before half of the before/after table without retrofitting instrumentation under time pressure.
Model gateway, routing, fallbacks, canaries (topic 55): the LiteLLM proxy in front of the Kaupex stack is where routing rules and per-tenant budgets actually get enforced, not in application code.

Production Python (topics 25 and 26): asyncio fan-out with bounded concurrency, connection reuse, exponential backoff with jitter, and resumable jobs - batch backfills are a job-scheduling problem before they are an LLM problem.
Basic statistics literacy: paired comparison on the same items, and enough sense of confidence intervals to know that a 1-point move on 80 eval questions is noise while a 9-point move is a result.

subtopics.name: Instrument the ledger before you change one line of prompt
subtopics.learn: Write every request to a `llm_calls` table with request_id, tenant_id, feature, model, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, ttft_ms, total_ms, stop_reason, and a prompt_version hash. Derive cost in a single pure function `cost(model, usage) -> Decimal` fed by a checked-in price table, never by hard-coded constants sprinkled through the code. Reconcile that derived number weekly against the Usage and Cost Admin API (`/v1/organizations/usage_report/messages` and `/v1/organizations/cost_report`, Admin key required, workspace-scoped keys will not work); if your ledger and the invoice disagree by more than a couple of percent you are missing a call path. Optimising without this table means you will 'save 40%' and be unable to prove it.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Usage and Cost Admin API

subtopics.name: Token accounting and pre-flight estimation
subtopics.learn: Use `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` with the exact same `model`, `system`, `tools` and `messages` you intend to send, so a large retrieval payload is priced before it is spent and can be rejected at the door rather than blowing a per-request budget. Internalise the asymmetry: output tokens cost about 5x input tokens on every current Claude model, so a 400-token answer can outweigh a 6,000-token context, and 'trim the system prompt' is usually the wrong first move. Know that `usage.input_tokens` in a cached response excludes cached tokens - total input is `cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens` - and that summing only `input_tokens` will silently under-report your spend by an order of magnitude once caching is on.

subtopics.name: Decompose latency: TTFT, TPOT, and everything that is not the model
subtopics.learn: Split end-to-end latency into queue/network time, time to first token (dominated by prefill over the whole prompt), inter-token latency multiplied by output length (decode), and your own post-processing. Learn to read the shape: a TTFT that scales with prompt size is a prefill problem (cache it, shrink it), a total time that scales with answer length is a decode problem (cap `max_tokens`, lower effort, shorten the output contract), and flat overhead is your infrastructure (TLS handshakes per call, cold Lambda, a synchronous retrieval hop). Measure at the client with a monotonic clock around the streaming iterator, recording the timestamp of the first `content_block_delta`, not the completed response.

resource.label: High Performance Browser Networking - Primer on Latency and Bandwidth

subtopics.name: Percentiles that survive review
subtopics.learn: Report p50/p95/p99 from histogram buckets, never from averaging pre-aggregated percentiles across pods - averaging quantiles is arithmetically meaningless and is the fastest way to lose credibility with a customer's SRE. Choose bucket boundaries that actually straddle your SLO (for TTFT: 100ms, 250ms, 500ms, 1s, 2s, 5s, 10s) because a p95 computed from three coarse buckets is a linear interpolation, not a measurement. Slice by feature and by tenant before you slice by nothing: a single p95 across a fast classifier and a slow summariser hides both. Always publish n alongside the percentile - a p99 over 200 requests is two data points.

subtopics.name: Prompt caching mechanics: cache_control, minimums, TTL, usage fields
subtopics.learn: Mark a content block with `"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}` to cache the entire prefix up to and including that block; the default lifetime is 5 minutes, refreshed for free on every hit, and measured from the start of the request that writes or reads it - a 4-minute streamed response burns 4 of those 5 minutes. Know that the minimum cacheable prefix is model-dependent (512 tokens on Opus 5, 1,024 on Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.8, 4,096 on Haiku 4.5) and that a shorter prefix silently does nothing: no error, no cache. Verify every time by asserting on `usage.cache_creation_input_tokens` and `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` - if both are 0 the block was never cached, which is the single most common reason a 'caching rollout' produces zero savings.

subtopics.name: Prompt layout for hit rate, and the invalidation table
subtopics.learn: The cache key is the literal prefix in the order `tools` -> `system` -> `messages`, matched byte-for-byte, so anything that varies per request (a timestamp, the user's name, a request id, a shuffled retrieval list) must live after your last breakpoint or your hit rate is zero. Memorise the invalidation rules that bite: editing any tool definition (name, description, or schema) invalidates the whole cache; toggling web search or citations invalidates system and messages; changing `tool_choice` or adding/removing an image anywhere invalidates messages; changing thinking config or `output_config.effort` invalidates message blocks. You get at most 4 explicit breakpoints (top-level automatic caching consumes one of the 4, and a 5th returns a 400) - spend them on boundaries between content of genuinely different change frequency: tools, static instructions, retrieved corpus, conversation tail.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Tool use with prompt caching

subtopics.name: Multi-turn incremental caching, 1-hour TTL, and pre-warming
subtopics.learn: For growing conversations, put `cache_control` at the top level of the request body (automatic caching) so the breakpoint tracks the last cacheable block as turns accumulate, or place explicit breakpoints yourself when different sections change at different rates. Reach for `{"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}` when the gap between turns exceeds five minutes - it doubles the write price (2x base input versus 1.25x) so it only pays off when the prefix is large and reuse is certain; when mixing TTLs, the 1-hour entries must appear before any 5-minute entries in the prompt. Pre-warm before a burst with a `max_tokens: 0` request whose breakpoint sits on the last block shared with real traffic (not on the placeholder user message) and with identical thinking and effort settings, otherwise you pay for a cache entry your production traffic never hits.

resource.label: Claude Docs - Prompt caching (automatic caching, TTL, pre-warming)

subtopics.name: Cache break-even arithmetic, and when caching loses money
subtopics.learn: Write the formula down and keep it in the repo: with a prefix of N tokens, a write costs 1.25N (or 2N at 1h) and each hit costs 0.1N against a baseline of N per request, so k requests within the TTL cost `1.25N + 0.1N(k-1)` cached versus `kN` uncached - break-even is just above k = 1.2 for the 5-minute cache and roughly k = 2.2 for the 1-hour cache. Then apply the real-world discount: your actual saving is `hit_rate` times the theoretical maximum, and hit rate is what your prompt layout and traffic shape determine. Compute the two numbers that decide whether to bother: cached prefix as a fraction of total input tokens, and input cost as a fraction of total cost - if 80% of your spend is output tokens, a perfect cache changes almost nothing and you are optimising the wrong half of the bill.

subtopics.name: The Message Batches API and what it actually guarantees
subtopics.learn: `POST /v1/messages/batches` takes up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever comes first, at 50% of standard prices, with most batches finishing inside an hour but a hard 24-hour expiry - results become available when all requests complete or at 24 hours, whichever is first. Poll `processing_status` until it flips from `in_progress` to `ended`, then stream the `.jsonl` from `results_url` rather than downloading it whole. Each result carries a per-request type of `succeeded`, `errored`, `canceled` or `expired`, and you are not billed for canceled or expired requests - which also means a job that quietly expires produces a silent gap in your output, not an error. Note that `max_tokens: 0` is rejected inside a batch, so cache pre-warming is not a batch trick.

subtopics.name: Designing batch jobs that are resumable and reconcilable
subtopics.learn: Make `custom_id` a deterministic function of your domain key (it must match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$`), for example `sha1(tenant:doc_id:prompt_version)[:32]`, so the same input never gets processed twice and results join back to your rows without an ordering assumption - batch results are not returned in submission order. Persist the batch id, the submitted key set, and a per-key status the moment you submit, then reconcile submitted-versus-returned after `ended` and requeue `expired` and retryable `errored` entries in the next batch. Triage workloads honestly: evals, backfills, bulk classification, document enrichment and nightly summarisation are batchable; anything a human is waiting on is not, and 'we'll batch the chat endpoint' is how you turn a latency complaint into an outage.

resource.label: Claude API Reference - Create a Message Batch

subtopics.name: Model tiering and cascade routing
subtopics.learn: Stop treating the model as a global constant. Classify each call site by what it actually demands - extraction, classification and routing usually hold on the small model; multi-step reasoning, ambiguous synthesis and code generation usually do not - and set the model per call site behind the gateway, not in scattered application code. Implement a cascade where the small model runs first and escalation is triggered by a machine-checkable signal (schema validation failure, a refusal, a self-reported confidence field, a retrieval-support check), then compute the blended cost: `p_escalate` above roughly 0.35 usually makes the cascade more expensive and slower than just calling the big model once. Measure escalation rate per category, because a cascade with a 70% escalation rate on legal questions is a cascade you should turn off for legal questions only.

subtopics.name: Output-token discipline: max_tokens, effort, stop conditions
subtopics.learn: Since output is the expensive half, attack it directly: set `max_tokens` to a real ceiling rather than the model maximum, use `output_config.effort` (low/medium/high on supported models) to cut how many tokens Claude spends before answering, and use `stop_sequences` where the output has a hard terminator. Alarm on `stop_reason == "max_tokens"` - a truncated answer is a paid failure and, if you retry it, you paid twice for one wrong answer. Instruct for brevity in the contract, not in adjectives: 'answer in at most 3 bullets, no preamble, no restatement of the question' reliably outperforms 'be concise'. Critically, changing effort or thinking config invalidates cached message blocks, so an effort experiment and a caching rollout must not ship in the same change or you will not know which one moved the number.

subtopics.name: Structured output as a cost lever
subtopics.learn: Prose answers pay for connective tissue you then throw away with a regex. Constrain the response to a schema - structured outputs or a tool schema with `tool_choice` forcing a single tool - so the model emits only the fields you consume, which typically removes 30-60% of output tokens on extraction and classification work while simultaneously removing your parsing failure mode. Design the schema for cheapness as well as correctness: enums instead of free text, short field names, no 'explanation' field unless a human actually reads it, and no repetition of input back into the output. Remember the caching interaction from the invalidation table: tool definitions sit at the very front of the cache prefix, so a one-word tweak to a tool description invalidates every cache entry you have.

subtopics.name: Streaming: fixing perceived latency without fixing latency
subtopics.learn: Set `"stream": true` and consume the SSE event sequence (`message_start`, `content_block_start`, `content_block_delta`, `content_block_stop`, `message_delta`, `message_stop`); read final token counts from the `message_delta` event's `usage`, and note that `message_start` already carries input and cache token counts so you can log cost before generation finishes. Streaming does not reduce total time or cost by a single token - it converts an 8-second blank screen into 700ms to first word, which is the metric users actually complain about. Know where it breaks: buffering proxies and some CDN configurations coalesce the stream and hand you the whole body at the end, so verify TTFT through the real ingress and not against localhost, and know that long non-streaming requests are also the ones most likely to hit gateway idle timeouts.

subtopics.name: Context compaction: stop paying to resend history
subtopics.learn: Long agent loops re-send every prior tool result on every turn, so cost grows quadratically in turn count even before quality degrades. Apply, in order: clear or truncate stale tool results (context editing), summarise older turns into a compact state block, cap retrieved chunks by a token budget rather than a fixed k, and drop raw payloads that the model has already extracted from. Every one of these edits rewrites the prompt prefix and therefore invalidates the message cache from the edit point forward - so compact at deliberate checkpoints (say, every N turns) rather than continuously, and measure the combined effect, because naive per-turn pruning can cost more in cache misses than it saves in tokens.

subtopics.name: Concurrency, rate limits, and the throughput ceiling
subtopics.learn: Limits are enforced per model class as RPM, ITPM and OTPM using a continuously-replenishing token bucket, so a burst of 200 parallel calls fails differently than the same volume spread over a minute. On a 429, honour the `retry-after` header and back off with jitter; steer proactively off `anthropic-ratelimit-input-tokens-remaining` and `anthropic-ratelimit-output-tokens-remaining` rather than waiting to be rejected. Two traps worth memorising: the spend-cap 429 carries no `retry-after` and will never succeed on retry until the next billing period, so your SDK's automatic retries will burn your entire timeout budget on a certainty; and a cache entry only becomes available once the first response has begun, so fanning out 50 identical-prefix requests at t=0 pays 50 cache writes instead of 1 write plus 49 reads.

subtopics.name: The non-regression gate for a model downgrade
subtopics.learn: A downgrade is only shippable with a paired comparison: same eval items, same prompts, same temperature, incumbent versus candidate, reported per category rather than as one mean. Define the acceptance band before you run it (for example: overall within 2 points, no single category down more than 5 points, zero regressions on the safety and refusal subsets) so you cannot rationalise afterwards. Expect prompts to be model-specific - a prompt tuned on the large model often needs more explicit structure and few-shot examples on the small one, and 'Haiku failed' frequently means 'we did not re-tune the prompt'. Wire the comparison into CI as a job that fails the PR and attaches the before/after table, so the cost saving cannot silently decay when someone edits the prompt three weeks later.

subtopics.name: Unit economics and the customer-facing number
subtopics.learn: Customers do not budget in tokens; they budget in units of work. Define the denominator with them - cost per resolved ticket, per compiled task, per document processed, per seat per month - and report cost per unit plus p95 latency as the two headline numbers, with token counts as supporting detail. Set the same shape as an SLO with an error budget (for example: p95 TTFT under 1.5s, cost per compiled task under $0.08) so a regression is an alert rather than a surprise on the invoice, and enforce per-tenant budget caps at the gateway with a graceful degrade path (downgrade the model, disable enrichment) instead of a hard failure. Always attach the quality delta to the cost delta in the same table: a saving reported without an eval number reads as a risk, not a win.

outcomes: You can produce a per-feature cost breakdown for a running system from your own `llm_calls` ledger and reconcile it to within 2% of the Usage and Cost Admin API figures for the same period.

You can raise the prompt cache hit rate on a real workload above 80% and prove it from `cache_read_input_tokens / (cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens)`, not from an assumption that caching is on.

You can state the caching break-even from memory (1.25x write, 0.1x read, so roughly 1.2 reuses within the 5-minute TTL; 2x write, so roughly 2.2 reuses at 1h) and decide whether a given call site should be cached at all.

You can convert an offline workload to the Message Batches API with deterministic `custom_id`s, reconcile submitted against returned keys, requeue `expired` and `errored` entries, and show the 50% price reduction as a line in the ledger.
You can cut Kaupex model spend by at least 30% with the eval delta inside a pre-declared acceptance band, and name which change produced which fraction of the saving.
You can look at a latency histogram and say within five minutes whether the bottleneck is prefill, decode, or your own infrastructure, and name the specific lever for each.

You can debug a caching rollout that produced zero savings by checking, in order: prefix below the model minimum, per-request content ahead of the breakpoint, a tool-definition or effort change invalidating the prefix, and parallel cold-start fan-out.
You can present a one-page before/after table to a customer stakeholder with cost per unit of work, p50/p95 latency, eval score by category, and sample size, and defend every cell.
failureModes: A request id, a `datetime.now()` stamp, or the user's name is interpolated into the system prompt ahead of the cache breakpoint, so every request writes a fresh cache entry and the 'caching optimisation' raises the bill by 25%.

The cached prefix is 700 tokens against a model with a 1,024-token minimum, so caching silently no-ops with no error returned, and nobody notices for a month because the code never asserts on `cache_read_input_tokens`.

Someone fixes a typo in a tool description, which invalidates the entire cache prefix for every tenant at once, and the resulting stampede of cache writes shows up as a cost spike that gets blamed on traffic growth.

A latency experiment toggles `output_config.effort` or thinking config per request, which invalidates message-block caches, so the effort A/B test and the caching rollout silently cancel each other out and the team concludes caching does not work.

A nightly batch backfill hits the 24-hour expiry, the `expired` results are never reconciled against the submitted key set, and a few thousand documents are permanently missing from the index with no error anywhere in the logs.

The service hits its monthly spend cap and returns 429s with no `retry-after`; the SDK's automatic retries hammer a certainty, requests pile up behind the retry budget, and a billing limit presents as a full outage.

The team downgrades to a smaller model on the strength of a 60-question aggregate score, and the regression that only existed in the 8-question refusal subset ships to production as a compliance incident.
interviewQuestions: A customer's monthly bill for your assistant tripled with flat request volume. Walk me through your diagnosis in order, and tell me what data you need in place beforehand for that diagnosis to take minutes instead of a week.
Explain prompt caching to their platform architect: what is the cache key, what invalidates it, what does it cost to write versus read, and at what reuse count does it stop being worth doing?

Design the request path for a support assistant with a 40,000-token policy corpus, 2,000 tenants, and a p95 TTFT budget of 1.5 seconds. Where do your cache breakpoints go, what is cached per tenant versus shared, and what happens at 09:00 when every tenant arrives cold at once?

You want to move from the large model to the small one to save 60%. What exactly do you run before you propose it, what is your acceptance band, and what do you tell the customer if the small model is 3 points worse overall but 9 points worse on multi-hop questions?
When is a cascade (small model first, escalate on failure) more expensive than just calling the large model, and how would you compute the escalation-rate threshold for a specific workload?
You enabled caching and the bill did not move. Give me the five things you check, in the order you check them, and the exact field you look at for each.
Which parts of this pipeline would you move to the Batch API, which would you refuse to move, and what breaks operationally when a batch expires at 24 hours instead of completing?
proofOfWork: Build `llm-cost-lab`: a small repository that runs one fixed workload from the Kaupex Task Compiler under six named configurations - baseline, caching only, caching plus structured output, small model only, cascade with escalation, and batch for the offline half - through a single `make bench CONFIG=<name>` entrypoint that writes every call to a SQLite ledger and emits a generated markdown report. The report must contain one row per configuration with columns for cost per unit of work, total input/cache-write/cache-read/output tokens, cache hit rate, p50 and p95 TTFT, p95 end-to-end latency, eval score overall and by category, escalation rate where applicable, and n - every cell traceable to a stored run_id. Include three things that prove you measured rather than assumed: a plot of cost per request against cache hit rate as the inter-request gap sweeps past the 5-minute TTL boundary; a break-even chart for 5-minute versus 1-hour TTL as a function of reuse count for your actual prefix size; and a deliberate negative result documented in the README, such as a configuration where caching or cascading cost more, with the arithmetic explaining why. Add a CI job that fails the build if cost per unit rises more than 10% or any eval category drops more than 5 points, plus a two-page COST-REVIEW.md written for a non-engineer stakeholder that leads with cost per resolved unit and the quality delta, not with tokens.
